post.name: Can the lottery system work in the US for pre-orders regarding consoles if enforced by retailers?
post.body:
I know that the Zelda themed Switch 2 for example was scalped before anyone had the opportunity to even place a pre-order. During the anticipation of the original Switch 2 (日本語・国内専用) in Japan on 2025, at the time: you can only register via a lottery system (you must have an active NSO membership and 50+ hours of gameplay for eligibility) and the retailer will only respond if you're being selected via the raffle.  

The lottery system is standard in Japan for basically anything on demand, to curb scalpers and FOMO meaning its complete R&G if you're even going to receive the product in question. If not, you re-register in a second lottery at another merchant or try your odds. Do you think the same or similar approach will work in the US or is it going to fail if a store were to do this since they're not used to that form of item acquisition?

post.name: Attested identities in lemmy: questions about acceptance, censorship and accountability
post.body:
Hi! I am a researcher at the CISPA-Helmholtz-Institute for information security (https://cispa.de/en/people/kuennemann). I would like to get some community feedback on a project we are working on. I am a Lemmy-user myself, but of course I use my other account for lurking; this account is for my research business.

My question taps into the age-verification debate, which I know is very controversial, and people are sceptical for very good reasons; I just ask everyone to stay polite and engage the topic. 

In short, I am worried about the effect bots have on public discourse, which to a large part takes place in the Internet. I would like to propose cryptographic methods that allow an instance to attest that a poster or commenter are a real human being. I think the European Unified ID (euid.eu) provides good infrastructure to do that, at the cost of relying on the member countries to provide them with an ID. Crypto-magic can (potentially - I haven't worked out the details yet) ensure that:

 - users from an instance that opted in are sure to belong to someone with an id, other instances may use this knowledge in their moderation tools
 - users from that instance can retain several pseudonyms that even this instance cannot link. Yet (configurable) policy can ensure that no users uses two pseudonyms in the same thread
 - we could cap how many posts or comments a user makes per day/week/month, across their pseudonyms
- users who post on this instance but are not displayed (in the web or to other instances) can provide evidence that they are being censored, which the public may review to discredit that instance and chose a new one.
- the infrastructure also happens to allow for age verification (EUID can attest to statements like "this anonymous person is > 18"), and it could be part of an instance's policy. Thanks to lemmy's federated infrastructure, multiple verifying instances with different policies can exist. It's not a focus of mine, though – I think social networks should not exploit children or adults. 

Some of these ideas we have worked out (and tested on) reddit in [this article]( https://publications.cispa.de/articles/conference_contribution/TrollThrottle_---_Raising_the_Cost_of_Astroturfing/24613275), which was before Lemmy became popular and EUID was on the horizon.

I am interested in practical advice about who to talk to about engineering and how to best involve the community – we've got a prototype fork of lemmy including end-user verifiable authentication. I am also interested in how the community feels about the burden of moderation and this as a potential remedy. When discussing age verification, some users say they will never accept any ID-based authentication. Are there some amongst those who would change their minds provided they had full pseudonymity and censorship could be detected and made public with cryptographically signed evidence?
